title: Iran War Pulls Last U.S. Carrier Out of Pacific, Opening Door for China
excerpt: The USS George Washington is leaving its patrol in the South China Sea to replace the battle-worn Lincoln in the Middle East, leaving no American aircraft carrier deployed in the Indo-Pacific for the first time in years.
body:
• The USS George Washington, based in Japan, is transiting from the South China Sea to the Middle East to relieve the USS Abraham Lincoln after its record-breaking 250-day deployment.
  • The move leaves no U.S. aircraft carrier deployed in the Indo-Pacific, where China has been actively projecting naval power and pressuring neighbors like the Philippines and Taiwan.
  • Analysts warn the Iran war's strain on the Navy could take three years to restore the fleet to its ideal readiness posture.
  • About 40% of U.S. Navy ships ready for operations are currently stationed in the Middle East, depleting both vessels and munitions earmarked for Pacific deterrence.

A Record Deployment Ends, a Void Begins

The U.S. Navy is preparing to swap out the USS Abraham Lincoln for the USS George Washington in the Middle East, U.S. officials told the Wall Street Journal. The Lincoln has been deployed for more than 250 days, spending 200 consecutive days at sea without a port call — a record for the modern Navy. Reports of food shortages, contaminated water, plumbing failures, and deteriorating morale aboard the ship prompted bipartisan concern in Congress.

https://x.com/USPacificFleet/status/2087979858970517683

Senator Richard Blumenthal wrote to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth citing "widespread reports of shortages of basic supplies, water contamination, plumbing issues, deteriorating mental health, deck safety concerns, and disruptions in the mail system." A person went overboard the Lincoln in early August but was quickly rescued.

Defense Secretary Hegseth dismissed the concerns as "completely misrepresented" and said the U.S. could maintain its blockade of Iranian ports indefinitely by rotating ships.

The Pacific Gap

But it is the George Washington's departure from Asia that carries the larger strategic consequence. The carrier had been operating in the South China Sea, making port calls in Vietnam and conducting patrols designed to counter Chinese influence and reassure allies like the Philippines and Japan.

"Normally, the George Washington would do its patrol and go and show the flag and demonstrate our resolve and our support to countries like the Philippines and Japan," Bryan Clark, a former naval officer and senior fellow at the Hudson Institute, told the WSJ. "We're going to forgo all these strategic opportunities to influence the relationships with the neighbors there."

The Washington recently transited the Strait of Malacca moving westward alongside guided-missile destroyers, according to ship-tracking data. Its departure leaves no U.S. aircraft carrier deployed in the Indo-Pacific — a region Washington's own national defense strategy, unveiled just months ago, designated as the key "geopolitical battleground."

China Watches Closely

About 40% of U.S. Navy ships ready for operations are currently stationed in the Middle East, according to the Center for Strategic and International Studies. The Abraham Lincoln and at least six missile destroyers based in Pacific ports were redirected to the Iran war theater earlier this year.

Japan has already faced delays in deliveries of hundreds of Tomahawk missiles ordered from the United States, according to Jan van Tol of the Center for Strategic and Budgetary Assessments. Taiwan's ruling party lawmakers have warned that Taipei must prepare for Beijing to step up "coercion" while the United States is distracted.

"The fleet is not sufficient to keep a steady presence in every theater."

— Bryan Clark, Hudson Institute

China has exploited previous episodes of U.S. distraction, noted Jennifer Parker, a former Royal Australian Navy officer and fellow at the Lowy Institute, pointing to Beijing's rapid militarization of South China Sea islands while Washington was focused on Afghanistan.

A Three-Year Hangover

The Navy has 11 active aircraft carriers, but only about eight are available for tasking at any given time. The Iran war has pushed the fleet into an unsustainable rotation cycle. The USS Gerald R. Ford completed the longest carrier deployment since the end of the Cold War — 11 months — before returning home in May.

Clark estimated it could take three years to restore the fleet to its ideal readiness posture. "If you've got two or three carriers on each coast that are in various stages of needing to be repaired or maintained, they're going to be waiting in line," he said.

The Iran war is also consuming munitions stockpiled for a potential Pacific conflict. Admiral Samuel Paparo, chief of U.S. Indo-Pacific Command, told the Senate Armed Services Committee that the military needs to "supercharge" its defense industrial base to replenish weapons being used at an unsustainable rate.

For allies across Asia, the question is no longer hypothetical. "The grand strategy is supposed to be 'contain Iran in the Middle East, then shift resources toward dealing with China,'" a Japanese ruling party lawmaker told Reuters. "But the question is whether there will be enough resources left to shift."
nri_angle: The strategic vacuum in the Indo-Pacific affects the security architecture that underpins trade routes and economic stability across Asia, with direct implications for countries with large Indian diaspora populations.
author: Diaspora Desk
